SOPR.SHOP — 5000+ LINE MASTER DEVELOPMENT PROMPT Complete website
builder platform inspired by modern no-code website builders Version:
1.0 Language of this specification: English Project owner: User-provided
project owner Primary domain requested: sopr.shop Primary goal: Build a
real, deployable, multi-user website builder, not a visual mockup.
IMPORTANT: Follow these requirements in order, and do not claim a
feature works until it has been implemented and tested. IMPORTANT: Never
expose private credentials, service-account keys, signing secrets, or
privileged API tokens in browser code. IMPORTANT: The Cloudinary API
Secret previously shared by the project owner must not be embedded in
this project; rotate it in Cloudinary if it may have been exposed.
IMPORTANT: Firebase web configuration is client configuration, not an
authorization mechanism; enforce authorization using Firestore Security
Rules and server-side checks. IMPORTANT: Free-tier availability, quotas,
domain support, and billing requirements can change. Verify current
provider requirements before deployment.

SECTION 01 — PRODUCT VISION Build SOPR.SHOP as a polished
website-building SaaS application. A new user must be able to register,
verify their email, create a website, edit it visually, preview it,
publish it, and download source files. The product must support both
beginner-friendly visual editing and advanced code editing. The product
must have a public marketing website, authentication pages, a user
dashboard, a website editor, published website pages, and an
administrator panel. The project must use a maintainable architecture
and documented setup. The application must not be a static demo with
fake buttons. Every visible interactive control must either work or be
clearly disabled with an explanation. When an integration is not
configured, show a useful setup message instead of pretending it
succeeded. Build the smallest complete vertical slice first, then expand
to the full feature set.

SECTION 02 — REQUIRED OUTPUT Deliver all application source files.
Deliver a README with setup instructions. Deliver an .env.example file
containing placeholder values only. Deliver Firebase initialization
code. Deliver Firestore Security Rules. Deliver Firestore index
configuration if required. Deliver Firebase Hosting configuration if
Firebase Hosting is selected. Deliver Cloud Functions source code if
server-side publishing or privileged actions require it. Deliver a
seed-data script or documented manual setup steps for starter templates.
Deliver automated tests for important application flows. Deliver
deployment instructions for the main app. Deliver deployment
instructions for the website publishing system. Deliver an explanation
of which features can operate on Firebase Spark and which may require
billing or another hosting design. Deliver an explicit list of remaining
limitations, if any.

SECTION 03 — TECHNICAL ARCHITECTURE Use React and Vite unless the
existing repository or environment strongly favors another supported
stack. Use JavaScript ES modules or TypeScript consistently; prefer
TypeScript for a larger production-oriented application. Use a routing
library with protected routes. Use Firebase Authentication for account
identity. Use Cloud Firestore for user profiles, website metadata,
project documents, template metadata, publishing records, and audit
records. Use Firebase Hosting for the application shell when
appropriate. Use Cloudinary for user media only after configuring safe
upload restrictions. Use EmailJS only for appropriate client-side email
workflows; never use it as proof that an email address is verified. Use
Firebase Authentication email verification as the authoritative
verification state. Use a ZIP-generation library such as JSZip for
client-side source exports when feasible. Use a mature code editor
component for advanced HTML, CSS, and JavaScript editing. Use a
drag-and-drop system that supports keyboard accessibility and stable
ordering. Use a component-based architecture. Separate presentation,
business logic, persistence, and provider integrations. Avoid putting
the entire application in one oversized source file. Do not create
unnecessary microservices. Prefer the simplest architecture that
satisfies the security and publishing requirements.

SECTION 36 — PUBLISHING ARCHITECTURE Design publishing before

serve published site documents through a controlled multi-tenant
renderer. Option C: use a backend or hosting provider designed for
dynamic multi-tenant sites. Do not assume one Firebase Hosting site

SECTION 49 — FIRESTORE DATA MODEL Design a documented Firestore schema.
Use users/{uid} for user profiles. Use sites/{siteId} for website
project metadata and document references where appropriate. Use
sites/{siteId}/revisions/{revisionId} for revisions if using
subcollections. Use templates/{templateId} for template metadata. Use
publishedSites/{siteId} or a similarly controlled structure for
publication metadata. Use notifications/{notificationId} with
recipient-specific access rules. Use reports/{reportId} for abuse
reports if moderation is enabled. Use auditLogs/{logId} for trusted
administrative events. Choose field names consistently. Use server
timestamps for authoritative timestamps. Avoid storing large HTML
documents without size limits. Avoid storing binary files in Firestore.
Keep document sizes below current Firestore limits. Design for
pagination. Design queries around known access patterns. Add required
composite indexes.

SECTION 50 — FIRESTORE SECURITY RULES Deny access by default. Allow
users to read their own private profile. Allow users to update only
permitted profile fields. Prevent users from changing their role. Allow
users to read and write only their own draft sites. Validate the owner
UID on site documents. Prevent ownership changes through client updates.
Prevent clients from writing trusted admin audit events. Prevent clients
from publishing directly if publication requires privileged checks.

filters, sorting, and pagination. Editor: test selection, block
addition, property editing, ordering, undo, and redo. Preview: test
responsive viewports and editor-control exclusion. Publish: test
successful publication, failure, retry, and unpublish. Export: test ZIP
creation, required files, asset paths, and secret exclusion. Media: test
valid upload, invalid type, oversized file, and network error. Admin:
test authorized access and unauthorized access. Profile: test updates,
validation, and account settings. Notifications: test read state,
destinations, and access rules.

APPENDIX C — REQUIRED QUALITY GATES No known critical security issue may
be ignored. No private credential may be included in the client bundle.
No broad Firestore write rule may remain in production. No unverified
user may bypass the configured verification gate. No user may edit
another user’s private project. No user may self-assign administrator
privileges. No failed publish operation may be marked successful. No
export may contain service-account credentials. No custom code may run
with privileged dashboard access. No UI-only placeholder may be
described as a completed feature. No deployment limitation may be
concealed.

APPENDIX D — EXPECTED RESPONSE FROM THE CODING AGENT Before
implementation, summarize the architecture and any blockers. During
implementation, keep a checklist of completed features. After
implementation, list all generated files. After implementation, explain
Firebase setup. After implementation, explain EmailJS setup. After
implementation, explain Cloudinary setup. After implementation, explain
administrator setup. After implementation, explain publishing setup.
After implementation, explain custom-domain setup. After implementation,
explain source export. After implementation, provide build and test
commands. After implementation, report test results honestly. After
implementation, list incomplete features.

END OF CORE MASTER SPECIFICATION The detailed implementation matrix
below expands the requirements into explicit, testable feature
obligations. Each matrix item is an independent requirement, not
permission to ignore the security and architecture rules above.
